articles.text: Wells Fargo reopens, Bank of America and Citibank still closed Citibank at 333 Highland Avenue and Bank of America at 345 Highland Avenue are temporarily closed to customer traffic. Bank of America has been closed for nearly two years, and CitiBank recently closed. Wells Fargo Bank at 344 Highland Avenue reopened on Tuesday, January 25, after six days of closure due to staffing shortages. A spokesperson for Bank of America, Betty Riess, said that the closure of its branch in Piedmont in March 2020 was due to COVID and “the health and safety of associates and clients. Typically, our temporary closures have occurred in areas where we’re seeing fewer visits, or our staffing is not sufficient for a center to remain open,” she said. ATMs at all three branch banks are operational. Wells Fargo Bank is open from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. Monday through Friday. Citibank at 333 Highland Avenue and Bank of America next door, remain closed.

articles.text: School district drops COVID from list of required vaccines Three piedmont parent attorneys and two anti-vaccination non-profit organizations filed a lawsuit against the Piedmont Unified School District challenging its policy of requiring all students to be vaccinated against COVID. On January 13 Alameda County Superior Court Judge Brad Seligman temporarily halted enforcement of the Piedmont mandate which would have referred unvaccinated students to online independent study. In a regularly scheduled school board meeting tonight, the district plans to announce the COVID vaccine will be removed from the list of mandatory vaccinations for attendance. “At this time, the District finds no educational value in transferring vaccine-hesitant students into an Independent Study program when we are experiencing a remarkably high vaccination rate across all campuses,” the board document states. As of January 21, 59 students out of a total district enrollment of 2,340 were not yet vaccinated, including four preschoolers not yet age-eligible. articles.text: Healthcare company Curative has moved its testing location from Vista Avenue in front of City Hall to the Community Hall parking lot at 711 Highland Avenue. Curative has expanded its testing from two days a week, Sunday and Monday, to five days a week, Monday through Friday, 8 a.m. to 3 p.m. Walk-up registration is accepted, but because of high demand, appointments are strongly encouraged. Appointments are free for everyone, and medical insurance is not required to access a COVID-19 test. The test is a self-collected PCR test, and results should be available within 48 hours from the receipt of the sample. At the request of Piedmont City Council, Curative is currently working to expand testing to weekends as well. Appointments may be made by visiting www.cur.tv/piedmont.

articles.text: The City of Piedmont is currently accepting applications from residents who are interested in serving on City Council on an interim basis. The deadline to apply is Monday, January 31. Piedmont City Council held a special meeting on January 6 to determine the process by which it would fill a vacancy left by council member Tim Rood following his resignation on December 31, 2021. Council members chose to seek applications for appointment to City Council from residents, to serve as interim council member until the results of the general municipal election are certified on November 8. A resident must meet three requirements to apply for the position. First, the person must be a qualified voter in Piedmont; second, the person must not hold any other office or employment with the city; and third, the person must not be rendered ineligible due to the term limits provisions of the City Charter. Interested residents may submit applications electronically, or in-person to the City Clerk’s Office by 5 p.m. on January 31. Postmarks will not be accepted. City Council will interview candidates and applicants will have the opportunity to discuss their candidacy with council members. At a special meeting on February 7, each applicant will be asked to make a brief presentation to council members. Applications are available on the City website at https://piedmont.ca.gov and from the City Clerk’s Office. For more information on the application process, contact City Clerk John Tulloch at (510) 420-3041 or via email at jtulloch@piedmont.ca.gov. “I’ll be in the Counting House, counting all the money.”

articles.text: The Piedmont Fire Department issued a shelter in place advisory on Saturday morning for the area of Lakeview Avenue and Poplar Way, where multiple trees and wires were down due to high winds. Tree limbs were continuing to fall throughout the day, and Fire Department and Piedmont Police Department staff joined PG&E workers to ensure the safety of pedestrians and vehicles. Piedmont Public Works worked to clear trees in various hot spots throughout the city. Standby crews responded onsite at 9 p.m. Friday night after receiving calls about downed power lines and fallen trees, confirmed Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales. “Crews placed barricades, signage, and cleared branches where possible. By 5 a.m. they called additional staff and on-call contractors to assist with tree removal and to open blocked roadways,” Gonzales said. At least five city-owned trees fell during the Friday night storm, and many more privately owned trees fell or were severely damaged. By 2 p.m. Saturday, all known roadways were re-opened as Public Works crews, Police Department, and Fire Department finished clearing debris and other hazards. PG&E reported widespread damages and multiple power outages in Montclair and pockets of Piedmont. Wind gusts were reported at nearly 60 miles per hour, according to the National Weather Service.

articles.text: The 2021-2022 Piedmont Education Foundation Giving Campaign far surpassed its goal of raising $3 million for Piedmont schools. This year’s campaign generated a record $3.7 million with contributions from 1,200 families, also a record high. The results reflect a deep support of children and schools in Piedmont. This support is critical, as Piedmont schools count on Giving Campaign funds to support essential programs that provide a top-notch education for students. “Piedmont families are showing their gratitude for reopened schools, increased health and safety measures, and a return to the robust curriculum and individualized student attention that set our schools apart,” said Education Foundation Executive Director Heather Frank. The funds will help keep Piedmont’s student/teacher ratios low and will continue to support essential programs including libraries and librarians, art and music, S.T.E.A.M. training, electives, A.P. classes, counselors, and special education support. Funds will be allocated by a committee composed of Piedmont parents and community members, who will meet to learn more about the district’s needs and decide on the allocation of funds. A full report of how the funds will be allocated will be made available to the public. In an informal competition, parents of first grade students won the contest for the highest participation with 81% of families giving. They have won a taco truck party in the spring. The kindergarten parents at Wildwood School had the highest participation level of the year with 93% of families donating to the Giving Campaign. “We really appreciate the community’s support of this year’s Giving Campaign, which makes up about 8% of [the] school district’s annual budget,” said Giving Campaign Co-Chair Christine Wente von Metzsch. The campaign’s success is also due to both the staff at the Piedmont Education Foundation office and a dedicated committee of volunteers that worked for months. This year’s volunteer committee was one of the largest yet, with over 60 parents from across Piedmont’s schools. This year’s campaign team put up banners and signs at the schools, conducted community outreach, wrote letters and made phone calls, organized and spoke at numerous community events, ran mail and e-mail campaigns and text banks, spread the word via weekly messaging in school bulletins, class emails and local news outlets, amplified campaign messaging on PEF’s social media. They also distributed 760 Giving Campaign lawn signs and engaged in personal outreach to hundreds of donors. “The Giving Campaign is truly a community effort. The tremendous success of this year’s campaign is a resounding testament to the ongoing commitment and dedication of volunteers and the donors who consistently put our schools and kids first,” said Nicki Gilbert, Chair of the Education Foundation board. The Giving Campaign leadership team would like to extend their deep gratitude to the team at the Piedmont Education Foundation, the many volunteers who helped with the campaign, and the entire Piedmont community for supporting our schools.

articles.text: Schools are reopening after summer break, and it’s time to send your children to school. One has asthma, and the other a history of lung complications. You rest assured that their school is [using] every protective measure possible. Unfortunately. for the majority of non-Piedmont residents, this likely isn’t a safe assumption. The Piedmont Highlander had planned to run a story demanding action on the part of the school district, asking them to mandate the COVID-19 vaccine for all students and staff of Piedmont schools. However, on September 22, the school board satisfied this request before it was made. They ruled that all persons must provide proof of vaccination to attend class on campus. All U.S. public schools must follow suit and mandate the vaccine in the interest of their students and staff. Any attending student or instructing staff member should be held to a basic standard of expectation of consideration and respect. They must protect both themselves and the members of their communities by receiving full inoculation against COVID-19. The current widely implemented policy across California schools directed at teaching staff allows weekly testing as a valid substitute for proof of vaccination. The caveat that unvaccinated people must be tested weekly provides little assurance that those individuals will not be carriers and transmitters of the virus. In the six-day interim period between testing it is highly likely that an individual [can be] infected, remains asymptomatic, and proceeds to interact with others, unknowingly acting as a carrier and transmitting the virus, according to the CDC. According to its August 23 news release, the FDA fully approved the Pfizer COVID-19 vaccine for individuals 16 years of age and older. All three vaccines went through four stages of rigorous clinical trial prior to public release, as per the FDA standard, according to the National Institute of Health. Severe allergic reaction to any of the vaccines has occurred in roughly 2 to 5 million cases, according to the CDC. It is important to protect personal freedoms, but not without question. Personal freedoms extend as far as the person to whom they belong. The moment any action extends beyond the bounds of the individual, it becomes the concern of all those the action affects. Vaccination against COVID-19 easily breaches this threshold. Curiosity and caution are important practices, but hesitancy bred by misinformation is exceedingly dangerous, and no public institution should cater to this mentality. The COVID-19 vaccine is safe, and this must be regarded as fact, and policy decisions made accordingly. Even a high vaccination rate within a community [does not] remove all risk associated with exposure to the virus. Having received both doses of the vaccine nearly eliminates the chance of hospitalization in young people; however, it does not guarantee full immunity or prevent transmission, according to the CDC. Young people, upon infection, can become transmitters of the disease, hence posing a serious threat to the more vulnerable individuals they may interact with. It is the duty of able community members to protect their vulnerable counterparts – they rely on the fulfillment of this duty. Piedmont has helped set an important precedent. This article was originally published in the high school newspaper, The Piedmont Highlander, on January 18, 2022. Aryana Fisher, a junior at Piedmont High School, is Editor of Closer Look for TPH.

Personal freedoms extend as far as the person to whom they belong. The moment any action extends beyond the bounds of the individual, it becomes the concern of all those the action affects. Vaccination against COVID-19 easily breaches this threshold. Even a high vaccination rate within a community [does not] remove all risk associated with exposure to the virus. Young people, upon infection, can become transmitters of the disease, hence posing a serious threat to the more vulnerable individuals they may interact with. It is the duty of able community members to protect their vulnerable counterparts – they rely on the fulfillment of this duty. Piedmont has helped set an important precedent. articles.text: As discussed last month, the lasting value of an education in most cases has much more to do with the cognitive skills students develop than the subject matter students remember. The exception to this idea is elementary school where students learn essential skills like reading, spelling and arithmetic. Being able to express oneself in writing is much more important than remembering the enlightened aspects of Macbeth. Learning to solve problems logically is far more important than remembering how to use the quadratic equation. And developing memory techniques for languages is probably more important than remembering the conjugations of estar in the preterite. So, when we examine our students’ classes, we need to examine them in terms of what cognitive skills are being developed. Understanding and logic vs. memorization In high school math and science classes the most valuable skills a student can develop are the ability to build an understanding of a complicated idea as well as logical problem solving. But these will not develop automatically. Students need to focus on developing these skills or they may not gain these skills and might only rely on memory. Understanding is built one piece at a time When trying to understand a complicated concept, it will not come all at once. Complicated ideas have multiple facets and relationships, so we gain each piece a bit at a time. Math is language restricted to quantities Math has two parts, the language that describes quantities and their interactions as well as the logical process of deducing values and relationships. But let’s focus on the language part. Every equation is saying that two different things are the same size. Knowing the Why and How of each step Whenever you take a step in math or science, students need to know why they are allowed to do the step and how it is moving them closer to their goal. If you have an equation, that means two things are the same size. So, for every step in solving an equation, either you have to change both sides the same way, or you have to change the representation of one side, but not the value. Solve logically, not with memory or heuristics There are three approaches to solving a problem, using memory, heuristics or logic. Some students simply try to remember what they have been taught. This requires no understanding and the only skill that is being developed is memory. It is akin to being a trained seal. Heuristics are general problem-solving strategies. Using Heuristics is better than relying on memory, but not much better. The most useful way to solve a problem is to use logic. Next month: How to solve a problem using logic. articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. articles.text: Mark your calendar for February 4-6, when Piedmont High School students will present the Disney musical Beauty and the Beast. 2022. Directed by Amy Moorhead, the production features over 40 students in the cast and on crew. With choreography by Moorhead, and vocal direction by Amy Belles, the stage musical is based on the Academy Award-winning animated film. The stage version includes all of the wonderful songs written by Alan Menken and the late Howard Ashman, along with new songs by Menken and Tim Rice. The original Broadway production ran for over thirteen years and was nominated for nine Tony Awards, including Best Musical. The classic story tells of Belle, a young woman in a provincial town, and the Beast, who is really a young prince trapped under the spell of an enchantress. If the Beast can learn to love and be loved, the curse will end, and he will be transformed into his former self. But time is running out. If the Beast does not learn his lesson soon, he and his household will be doomed for all eternity. In a tale as old as time, the show is filled with spectacular costumes. It is a great opportunity to bring your entire family to the theater. Performances will take place at Holy Names High School’s theater at 4660 Harbord Drive in Oakland. Tickets are available online at https://www.showtix4u. com/events/pusdbeauty. articles.text: Piedmont Community Service Crew (PCSC) teen volunteers are currently assisting CityTeam Ministries with the renovation of a century-old building in Oakland that will be used for transitional housing and support for the homeless. PCSC is a youth-led coed service crew with the Piedmont Scout Council led by Ken Li, who created the crew in 2004. Crew members, mostly high school students, participate in several ongoing and recurring service programs, the most recent being assisting CityTeam. “CityTeam Ministries recently started a major upgrade project and put out a call to volunteers to help them with their work in order to keep their costs at a minimum,” said Ken Li. “Through our long-standing relationship with Rebuilding Together Oakland, PCSC heard about this opportunity. We jumped at the chance to make a big impact where our teen members can learn some hands-on skills while helping CityTeam.” Crew members have visited the site twice this month, and last Sunday, January 23, a small group of PCSC teens cut and hung drywall, patched holes in the plaster, and sanded previous coats of drywall. “Young people can have very little experience doing this. Some kids have done drywall work before, but for many it’s very new. We pride ourselves in giving [PCSC crew members] opportunities like this,” said Li. “Service work often revolves around learning a new skill,” Li added, “like cooking, gardening, and home improvement.” The building on Washington Street serves the Oakland community in many ways. At that location CityTeam volunteers offer hot meals every weekday night, and bagged lunches and meals on Saturdays and Sundays. Clean showers are available also. The nonprofit CityTeam helps to relieve the many challenges that low-income Oakland families face. PHS Junior and PSCS crew member Elena Blanco measures drywall. Josh Sachs prepares to install new drywall on a home on Washington Street in Oakland. PCSC crew member Ethan Tran and Elena Blanco carry ladders while assisting in the renovation of a home on Washington Street in Oakland. Ethan Tran “It really is an amazing place, where lives are restored. However, that couldn’t be done without all of the amazing volunteer help,” said Becky McKeen, a Piedmont resident who is an administrative assistant for CityTeam. Ethan Tran, a Piedmont High PCSC crew members Amy Derr and Sara Broach are taught how to safely use power drills. School junior who assisted in last weekend’s service excursion, offered his insight on the experience. “It was a really wonderful experience working at the CityTeam project. I had a great time learning new skills. Learning the backstory of the building inspired me to work harder and hopefully help out again,” he said. “I learned how the leader of the project was formally incarcerated and how this building helped him, and many other people who had fallen on harsh times, move on with their lives.” Li added that his hope is for the Community Service Crew to volunteer at least once each weekend for the next several weeks. articles.text: This treasure of California is among the best winter hikes of the Sierra Nevada Mountains. The abandoned railway at Donner Pass, originally constructed in 1867 for the Central Pacific Railroad’s portion of the First Transcontinental Railroad, is a serene wintertime hike. The trek takes you through hollowed out mountain tunnels and snow sheds through the pass surrounding Donner Lake. Aside from the obvious historic railway, the mountain pass is the same area where the Donner Party met their fate in the fierce winter of 1846 – becoming the namesake of the lake and surrounding state park. The walk through the train tunnels is brief, just 2.1 miles, but it gives you the magic of the Tahoe winter without getting knee deep in snow. It’s a great place for children, families, and beginning snowshoers. During warmer weather, you can walk past the last snow shed and up to Donner Peak. Taking the same route as our 2018 summer visit, we go from McGlashan Point over a Native American petroglyph site The starting point for the trail from McGlashan Point goes up a popular sledding hill to the China Wall and first tunnel. Snow piles into some sections of the Donner Pass trail. TJ Stevko, CFP® Financial Advisor 370 Highland Avenue Suite 201 Piedmont, CA 94611 510-547-4589

articles.text: 4-1 win over Arroyo, 3-1 loss to non-league Acalanes Piedmont’s girls’ soccer team was victorious 4-1 over nonleague opponent Arroyo on Friday, January 21 at Estuary Park in Alameda, but they took a 3-1 loss to Acalanes in Lafayette on Monday, January 24. Piedmont has seven matches left in the season, all against Foothill Division opponents. The six-team league with Berkeley, Castro Valley, Bishop O’Dowd, San Leandro, and Alameda is always a tight race. Piedmont’s cur rent record against league teams puts them in the running for a league title and this year will likely be another photo finish. “Everyone has beaten everyone in the league. We still have games against everyone and still haven’t faced Bishop O’Dowd. It’s really close,” said coach Dan Chubbock, who won his first Foothill banner in 2018. PHS has two matches with Bishop O’Dowd after the first game was postponed due to COVID-19 outbreak at O’Dowd . The teams play one another this Friday, January 28 and again on Monday, February 7. “It’s very, very tight. Friday’s game is probably going to determine whether we have a chance at winning the league title. The result on Friday will have a very big impact on the league. Berkeley just beat O’Dowd, so that puts them in the running,” said Chubbock. Staff Photos Piedmont holds a 4-3-2 record and has seven matches remaining, all against league competition. 3-1 loss to Acalanes Piedmont traveled to Lafayette on Monday, January 24 to face Acalanes, losing 3-1. The Dons compete in Div. 3 in the North Coast Section, while PHS plays in Division 2. The Highlanders trailed 1-0 after seven minutes and conceded a second goal around the 35th minute after the Dons’ forward attempted a cross which arced into the net. Junior midfielder Audrey Lam landed Piedmont’s first goal on a beautiful shot from 25 yards to the top bin to make it 2-1 with 15 minutes left in the game. “It was a great goal. She cut inside from the left and smashed it to the top corner,” said Chubbock. Acalanes went on to score their final goal about five minutes later. 4-1 win over Arroyo Piedmont outplayed Arroyo of San Lorenzo 4-1 in a game at Estuary Park in Alameda on January 21. PHS led 2-0 by halftime and pulled ahead 3-0 in the second half before Arroyo pulled closed 3-1, but Highlanders added one more in the closing minutes. Goals were scored by junior Cameron Lorin had two goals, while Rachael Barton, and Hailey Marshburn also scored. He helped Stanford wins Pac-12 championships in 2018 as a freshSeptember 26. Recently on January 16 at the Cal Winter Invitational, Thiel and Julia Rosenqvist defeated Santa Clara’s Katherine Petty and Lindsey Pesqueira, 8-4. Thiel also competed in singles, beating Saint Mary’s Olivia Rook, 6-2, 6-4. On January 15, Thiel and Hannah Viller Moeller beat Cal Poly’s Eliza Bates and Sherya Ravilla, 8-4. She also beat Bates in singles, 6-2, 6-3. She and Viller Moeller opened the Winter Invitational on January 14 with a 8-5 win over Stefanie Silva and Gabriela Tevez. articles.text: Featuring Symphony in C, Trio, and world premiere of Mrs. Robinson Photo by Erik Tomasson Dores André and Lonnie Weeks rehearsing as Mrs. Robinson and Benjamin in Cathy Marston’s new ballet, Mrs. Robinson. San Francisco Ballet will present Program I, a selection of three productions, beginning February 1 and running through February 12. George Balanchine’s masterful Symphony in C, with the music of Georges Bizet, will begin the program and includes more than 50 San Francisco Ballet dancers onstage. Trio, choreographed by Artistic Director Helgi Tomasson, includes the music of Tchaikovsky. The dancers will be adorned in billowing gowns and velvet jackets. The world premiere of Mrs. Robinson will complete the program. With a nod to the iconic American novella and film The Graduate, Cathy Marston’s retelling is from the perspective of the titular seductress. “I immediately thought—this is it,” said Marston after learning the novella is set in San Francisco. “This is the piece that I need to make for San Francisco Ballet.” “In the film, Anne Bancroft is impenetrable. And that’s genius, because it means you project your own feelings onto hers. I suppose that was the inspiration for the ballet. I wanted to get underneath the surface and find out why Mrs. Robinson is as she is, why she does the things that she does, and make specific choices based on those answers,” she added. The music for Mrs. Robinson was composed by Terry Davies, with scenic and costume design by Patrick Kinmonth. San Francisco Ballet now requires proof of updated vaccination status to watch live performances. Patrons are also required to wear an N95, KN95, or KF94 mask to enter the venue; the ballet company will provide these masks to patrons if needed. Food and drinks will not be permitted inside the auditorium. There are multiple performance times between February 1 and 12. To see a full list, and to purchase tickets, visit https:// www.sf ballet.org/productions/ program-1/. Performances will take place at the War Memorial Opera House at 301 Van Ness Avenue in San Francisco. Tickets may also be purchased by calling (415) 865-2000.

articles.text: Christoph Waltz, Robert Pattinson, Reese Witherspoon, and Tai in Water for Elephants. Water for Elephants is a solid adaptation of the 2006 best-selling novel by Sara Gruen. The film opens with an old man (Hal Holbrook), standing out in the rain, watching the circus, now loaded on trucks, preparing to leave and move onto the next town. One of the circus owners brings him inside, and over a glass of whisky, curious about the old guy, encourages him to tell his story. And so the tale begins, told at first by the old Jacob, but then his voice over soon morphs into that of young Jacob (Robert Pattison), who is sitting for his final veterinarian exam. He is called out of the test and told that his parents have just been killed in a car accident. Devastated, Jacob packs his things and leaves, jumping a train, one that turns out to be carrying the Benzini Bros. circus. August Rosenbluth (Christoph p Waltz), the circus ringmaster and boss, hires Jacob as a circus roustabout, at least until he finds out that he is a vet. August’s wife, the lovely Marlena (Reese Withersoon), immediately captures Jacob’s attention. She performs center ring, of course, and the film soon telegraphs that a relationship is in the offing, the only question is how it will secretly evolve. There is much that makes this film more than just passable. One is the setting – a circus in 1931 during the depths of the Great Depression. It was a time when people were desperate for any form of entertainment, anything to take them out of the reality of that stark economic period. The Benzini Circus is replete with all manner of interesting characters. It is a world apart from the ordinary life led by those who live in the towns and bring their children to see the extraordinary. The circus is also a culture unto itself with a language and mores that are more than interesting. Unfortunately, the film only briefly touches on this world, though the opportunity is offered when an old veteran, Camel (Jim Norton), takes Jacob on a tour. He is dazzled and in awe of all that he sees. The circus is vibrant and alive, full of color and magic and music. But there is also a dark side, one that Jacob comes to understand and even fear. August, he discovers, can slip from friendly and welcoming to cruelty that borders on the insane. C h r i s t o ph Wa lt z , t he Oscar-winning actor who starred in Inglourious Basterds, delivers a superb performance, one that is powerful and captivating. He provides an interesting contrast to Pattison’s Jacob. Pattison’s face is not one that emotes. He doesn’t seem capable of changing his expressions from scene to scene, his remoteness ever consistent. It was a quality that worked nicely in the “Twilight” series where he portrayed a stoic vampire; however, in the role of Jacob he is asked to do more. Unfortunately, he seems somewhat at a loss. Witherspoon and Waltz are consummate actors and able to transform themselves. Waltz chews up every scene he is in, as he did in Inglourious Basterds where he convincingly portrayed a malevolent Nazi officer. Witherspoon is resilient and fragile with a touch of trapped desperation. In the aggregate Water for Elephants is fine entertainment. Water for Elephants. Directed by Francis Lawrence. Starring Reese Witherspoon, Robert Pattison, Christoph Waltz, Hal Holbrook and Jim Norton. 2 hrs., 3 min. Rated PG-13.

articles.text: California paella looks spectacular, and nothing could be easier to make. One of the most spectacular restaurants in the world is located not far from Barcelona. It is like eating in Mesa Verde amidst the cliff dwellings in New Mexico. Magnificent vistas and beautiful paella – need I say more? Let your imagination run wild. All of this is yours just about an hour from Barcelona. If you are religious, take the opportunity to visit the Montserrat monastery, then continue driving into the mountains. All the while think of paella. Set your compass to Restaurant El Puig de la Balma in the town of Mura. The location is stunning. It is a crevasse in a sheer mountainside. The restaurant itself was built in the 11th century entirely of rock. Take a look at its website and then study the cliff dwellings in New Mexico. California style paella In honor of Catalonians’ favorite dish, here is a California style paella. It is so simple that you don’t even need a recipe. You can serve any number of people by adjusting the portion of rice – one handful per person. It is best if you have a paella pan, but a large skillet will work just as well. Moisten in the pan with some good quality olive oil and then put in some salt and pepper. Meanwhile, dice some bell pepper, onion, and garlic and put them in the pan to brown. When the vegetables are soft, add the next ingredients. You may put in anything you have in the refrigerator. Some things you might use are artichoke hearts, olives, zucchini or any kind of vegetable, even capers. Anything goes. And you can use any kind of meat. To the lightly browned vegetables add a generous portion of arborio rice, one handful per person. 12 ounces will serve six people. You will need broth. Approximately 35 ounces of broth will be enough for six people. You may want to add a pinch or two of saffron but be sure to use good quality saffron. Bring this mixture to a rapid boil. After a few minutes you can add the meat. After about 15 minutes see if you need to add more broth. Add just enough to moisten what you are cooking. Cook another five or 10 minutes and check that the rice is tender enough for your taste. If it is done to your liking, remove it from the flame. I like to cook my paella a little longer and make it crisp on the bottom. For dessert a baked apple is typical. You could also serve chilled poached fruit. To add a perfect touch to the dinner, pour some Cune Reserva, an inexpensive Rioja wine from Spain. Better yet, you can make your paella dinner more elegant with a bottle of Lopez de Heredia Vina Tondonia, a world class Rioja. And now for some music On a personal note: Because of the usual suspects (COVID), my concert entitled “It Ain’t Baroque”, originally scheduled for January 30 at the Piedmont Center for the Arts, is being postponed until the weekend of April Fool’s Day. There is humor in this… and more is yet to come.

articles.text: Bu Jim Gardner Dear Jim: I have lived in my home for 30 years and all of a sudden, I’m starting to have a bunch of problems. My basement and crawlspaces are flooding, and I’m getting cracks in the walls and ceilings in my house. Why is this happening, and what can I do about it? I have talked to several drainage people, and they have told me The correct solution different things. –Alex S. Dear Alex: Most older homes have inadequate or non-existent drainage systems, that are original to the property or improperly built and are no longer working. Add to that the effects of a changing climate and more substantial rain events, and our homes are no longer able to cope. Cracks, sloping floors and other interior changes are often merely a reflection of drainage-related settlement problems when our foundations are not built to modern standards. Older foundations are shallow, unreinforced, in poor condition and more prone to movement and water infiltration. A dual drainage membrane system helps preserve older foundations. It is crucial to identify the particular type of drainage issue you are experiencing. Water problems can be a function of either surface water, subterranean water, or both. The solutions range from simply attaching flexible pipe to your downspouts to get water away from your house, to digging 10’ deep trenches when French drains are needed for deep drainage issues. Where the drainage work is located, what type of system to use, and the drainage depth are different for every project and are a function of the particular conditions at your home. Hillside homes on steep slopes with water problems in different locations can be a challenge. Unfortunately, many drainage “professionals” offer up cookie cutter solutions that can create more substantial drainage problems in the future if they are not properly designed. What should I do about It? Sometimes the answer is to do nothing. If you are a new homeowner and the problem is not an emergency, I often recommend observing the problems through a full rain cycle. If downspouts are draining up against the house, flexible piping should be attached to them so water is brought away from the house. If the issues are Separate piping for downspouts and the French drain are essential. ongoing or more urgent, I would consult with an experienced drainage contractor. articles.text: Longtime Piedmont resident Nicholas Molnar, a vintner who helped pioneer fine wine in the now-famous Napa County region of Carneros, died on January 11. He was 94. A native Hungarian who fled Budapest after the 1956 revolution failed to overthrow the Stalinist regime, Molnar was an entrepreneurial grape grower, planting numerous vineyards in Napa County in the 1960s and ’70s. Presciently, in 1973 he bought a 100-acre plot in what were then viewed as the marginal southern stretches of the county, abutting the marshlands of San Pablo Bay. The climate there was considered too windy, too cold, too extreme for fine wine. Today, Carneros is renowned as one of California’s premier places for wine grapes, and that vineyard became the foundation for the Molnar family’s Obsidian Wine Co. “He was always an explorer,” said Arpad Molnar, his son. Later in his career, working with his children, Molnar planted a vineyard in another place that was considered marginal, Lake County, and became one of the first to import Hungarian oak barrels into the U.S. As with the Carneros vineyard, these ventures were initially met with skepticism, but ultimately proved influential on the California wine industry. Molnár Miklós was born in Budapest in 1927. He grew up in a politically fraught time, as Hungary faced the Great Depression, then World War II, then Soviet occupation. Molnar’s father was a business owner — he ran a trucking company — and in the late 1940s, like many who were vilified as capitalists, both father and son spent time in prison. He married a gymnast, Andrea Bodo. While she was in Australia, competing in the 1956 Olympics, a revolt broke out in Budapest against the Soviet regime. Molnar participated, taking to the streets in October 1956. When it became clear that the Soviets would crush the revolution, Molnar fled, crossing the Austrian border on his own. He found his way to Melbourne, where he reunited with his wife, who had won a gold medal. Molnar, Bodo and other members of the Hungarian Olympic gymnastics team decided not to return to Hungary, initially remaining in Australia. A new opportunity soon presented itself: U.S. magazine magnate Henry Luce, who had just founded a new publication called Sports Illustrated, offered to host the Hungarian team on a tour of the United States. (The move, Arpad Molnar believes, was politically motivated, publicizing the refugees of a communist regime during the height of the Cold War.) The arrangement proved especially advantageous for Molnar, who had done some work as a journalist in Hungary and was assigned to cover the tour for Sports Illustrated. Just before Christmas 1956, the tour touched down in San Francisco. “Gov. Knight Hails Stateless Group,” reads The Chronicle’s headline on Dec. 25. Molnar and Bodo immediately took to the city and decided to stay. In San Francisco, Molnar worked briefly as a journalist and then sold life insurance. He and Bodo divorced, and in 1967 he married another Hungarian refugee, Catherine de Bokay. They settled in Piedmont. “He had been a patriarch among Hungarian-Americans in the Bay Area, and could well have served as an honorary Hungarian consul here too, ready to answer any query about the old country, the culture or language while producing California wines with relish. I felt privileged to have known him over the past half-century here,” said Piedmont resident Paul Hertelendy, also of Hungarian ancestry. Among his life insurance customers were the Pepi brothers, who had a winery in Napa. (Originally called Robert Pepi Winery, it’s now Cardinale, owned by Jackson Family Wines.) That’s where Molnar got the idea to plant a vineyard, according to his son. He placed ads in newspapers to find investors. Beginning in the 1960s, aided by numerous investors, Molnar bought several undeveloped plots of land in Napa County and planted wine grapes on them. Not all of them worked out, and in several cases he ended up having to sell the properties to meet his obligations to investors. But one parcel, in the southern edge of the county where the Napa River meets the bay, he managed to keep. Before Molnar bought it in 1973, the 100-acre site had been sheep grazing land. Few other vineyards existed in Carneros at the time; it would be 12 more years before Carneros was officially recognized as an American Viticultural Area, the government designation for a wine region. Conventional wisdom held that it wasn’t as well suited to wine grapes as the rest of Napa County. Molnar proved otherwise. He planted Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, grape varieties that thrive in cooler climates. The same year, the French Champagne company Moet Hennessy arrived in Napa, with plans to create a winery – Nicholas Molnar helped pioneer fine wine in the now-famous Napa County region of Carneros. Famed California vintner Nicholas Molnar with wife Catherine. what would become Domaine Chandon – and was looking for Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, the grapes used in Champagne. Through 1985, Molnar sold the entire crop from his vineyard to Chandon. Today, the fruit is sold to sparkling-wine producers Schramsberg and Mumm, and also used for the Molnar family’s own Poseidon label. “He was always a bit of an outsider,” said Arpad Molnar. “The wine industry is so insular, and he sort of orbited around that scene, but never wanted to be in that scene. He always felt that when you’re outside of it a little bit, you can think creatively.” In the early 1990s, Molnar and his two sons, Arpad and Peter, became involved in efforts to revitalize Hungary’s economy after the fall of the communist regime. Molnar’s first idea: wild rice. “He read an article about wild rice in the San Francisco Chronicle and how popular it was becoming,” Arpad Molnar said. So he bought some, flew to Hungary, and helped farmers plant it in their fields. He had a similar idea about wine barrels after finding a cooperage in Hungary, called Kádár, that was struggling financially. Though it had once produced wine barrels, during the Soviet occupation it had been forced to make furniture for Russian markets. They decided to help by buying its barrels and importing them into the U.S. “Winemakers told us, no one here is ever going to buy a Hungarian barrel,” said Arpad Molnar. Then as now, California’s wine industry is modeled on France, growing French grapes — like Cabernet Sauvignon, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir — and aging them in French oak barrels, which many high-end wineries still consider the gold standard. When the Molnars imported their first Hungarian barrels in 1993, their main selling point was that they were cheaper than the French counterparts. At first, their only customer was Gallo. But once again, Molnar was ahead of the curve. The Molnars now sell Kádár barrels to 120 wineries in California and in countries including Australia and New Zealand. The family eventually took an ownership stake in the cooperage, adding an impressive partner — the famous French cooperage Taransaud. Molnar initially called his land in Carneros in 1973 the Chardonnay Vineyard. His children later convinced him to change the name to the less generic-sounding Poseidon Vineyard. Molnar’s last major frontier was in Lake County. By the late 1990s, land in Napa County was getting expensive, and he suspected that there was an opportunity to be had in the areas just north of the county line, where the terroir was similar but the real estate market much softer. Again with investors, he and his sons bought a 100-acre walnut orchard in 1999. The soil was studded with chunky, shiny, black obsidian rocks. They called the vineyard Obsidian Ridge, and soon developed a strong reputation for producing Napa Valley-caliber Cabernet Sauvignons. “None of this struck us until much later, but it was as outthere as planting in Carneros in the 1970s,” said Arpad Molnar. “Everyone said you couldn’t grow great Cabernet in Lake County.” His father would have wanted to be remembered as a pioneer, Arpad Molnar said. “He had this relentless curiosity. He was always interested in what was new, not quite there yet. Sometimes it didn’t work out. And sometimes it did.” Nicholas Molnar is survived by his wife, Catherine; his children Aniko, Peter and Arpad; and his grandchildren Renna, Kyla, Nichos, Gabriel, Eszter and Andreas. This obituary was principally written by Esther Mobley and appeared in the San Francisco Chronicle on January 23, 2022.

articles.text: Although the Bay Area has received substantial rainfall recently, Piedmont and the surrounding area of Alameda County are still in a severe drought according to the U.S. Drought Monitor and the East Bay Municipal Utility District. Recent weather has led to Alameda County experiencing an above average amount of rainfall. While recent rains aren’t enough to end the drought, there are ways to collect and utilize rain here in Piedmont. Rainwater is a renewable resource that can be harvested and recycled. Apart from the equipment necessary to catch and use the rain, such as a rain barrel, using rainwater is essentially free. Freshwater from rainfall can reduce the need for supplemental irrigation and contribute to resilient, climate-appropriate gardens. Harvesting rainwater is sustainable and can be implemented by anyone. monters can reduce dependence on municipally treated water throughout the year. During the summer months when water is in peak demand, using rainwater can save treated water for necessities. Rain barrels and rainwater catchment systems are available to purchase at local Bay Area hardware stores in a variety of sizes and styles. Local to the Bay Area, the Urban Farmer Store’s Rainwater Harvesting Resources, Greywater Action’s Presentations and Videos, and Garden for the Environment’s upcoming rainwater harvesting events can help Piedmonters learn about how to prepare their own rainwater harvesting system. Although there are many types of rain barrels and rainwater catchment systems to consider, the best system will vary depending on individual needs. There are a few key factors to consider Piedmont resident Julia Burke utilizes attractive ceramic “rain barrels” in her garden. when setting up a rainwater harvesting system. For example, research shows that the best rain barrels have thick walls that can withstand different temperatures, are opaque to inhibit algae growth, and are securely covered and screened to prevent debris, insects, and objects from falling into or even living in the tank. The barrel or system should be planned so that it is in a safe, stable, and secure spot to prevent erosion from overflow, tipping or movement of the barrel, or water concentrating near structures. Furthermore, for landscape irrigation purposes, the system will need to have an easy outlet nozzle or otherwise accessible hose or connection to a drip irrigation system. For those who already have rainwater harvesting systems, regular inspection, cleaning, and maintenance can prolong the life of your system. Rain gutters and water catchment systems should both be inspected and cleaned twice a year to ensure they are free of debris that may inhibit the harvesting system. When inspecting a rain barrel, make sure there are no cracks or algae inside the barrel and that the screen is capable of keeping out debris and insects such as mosquitos. Rain barrels should be cleaned once a year to prevent the buildup of debris, which can be removed with nontoxic cleaner like vinegar. Rainwater harvesting is just one part of a series of actions that can help conserve water. Other resources for Piedmonters to save water and utilize resources during times of drought include the Piedmont Climate Challenge and the Bay Area Stormwater Management Agencies Association (BASMAA). The Piedmont Climate Challenge highlights water-wise changes including mindful lifestyle changes as well as home appliance upgrades to maximize water efficiency. Similarly, the BASMAA website features Rain Barrel and Rain Garden Fact Sheets. With these actions in mind, Piedmonters can play their part in contributing to a sustainable water management system. For example, research shows that the best rain barrels have thick walls that can withstand different temperatures, are opaque to inhibit algae growth, and are securely covered and screened to prevent debris, insects, and objects from falling into or even living in the tank. The barrel or system should be planned so that it is in a safe, stable, and secure spot to prevent erosion from overflow, tipping or movement of the barrel, or water concentrating near structures. Furthermore, for landscape irrigation purposes, the system will need to have an easy outlet nozzle or otherwise accessible hose or connection to a drip irrigation system. For those who already have rainwater harvesting systems, regular inspection, cleaning, and maintenance can prolong the life of your system. Rain gutters and water catchment systems should both be inspected and cleaned twice a year to ensure they are free of debris that may inhibit the harvesting system. When inspecting a rain barrel, make sure there are no cracks or algae inside the barrel and that the screen is capable of keeping out debris and insects such as mosquitos. Rain barrels should be cleaned once a year to prevent the buildup of debris, which can be removed with nontoxic cleaner like vinegar. Rainwater harvesting is just one part of a series of actions that can help conserve water. Other resources for Piedmonters to save water and utilize resources during times of drought include the Piedmont Climate Challenge and the Bay Area Stormwater Management Agencies Association (BASMAA). The Piedmont Climate Challenge highlights water-wise changes including mindful lifestyle changes as well as home appliance upgrades to maximize water efficiency. Similarly, the BASMAA website features Rain Barrel and Rain Garden Fact Sheets. With these actions in mind, Piedmonters can play their part in contributing to a sustainable water management system. Even some large frozen sections of water created massive blocks of ice that are clear as a piece of glass. You’ll find few sites that combine history and artwork with graffiti covering each wall of the sheds – some pieces more magnificent in detail than others. Peeking around unsuspecting corners and behind walls, walkers with keen eyes can find some of California’s most prominent urban artists and large murals. Proper hiking gear is required at some ice-covered areas to prevent slipping and accidental falls. With limited parking at the entrance to the tunnels, some may have to park off the road along Donner Pass Road or at the Donner Lake Overlook parking lot. In our five miles of hiking, we passed just 27 hikers during our time in the tunnels. Another 13 were huddled around the starting area’s sledding hill toward the China Wall. To access this area, hikers can punch in Donner Pass, Summit Haus, or Donner Lake Overlook on their GPS device for common starting areas. Return in the summer to see petroglyphs along McGlashan Point and walk up to Donner Peak.
